sections.learningObjectives:
- Define HIPAA and protected health information (PHI) and identify covered entities and business associates.
- Apply the minimum necessary standard and distinguish permitted disclosures (TPO) from those requiring authorization.
- Describe patient privacy rights under the Privacy Rule and how the front office supports them.
- Recognize breach, enforcement, and penalty concepts and when to escalate privacy concerns.
- Apply reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to daily office tasks.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

HIPAA is a big rule book that protects people's private health details. Think of it like the rule that says your diary at the doctor's office is private and only certain people may read it.

### Question 2

The Privacy Rule is like a fence around your health information. It says: your health details belong to you, and the clinic must keep them private unless the rules say otherwise.

### Question 3

Every rule needs a referee. For HIPAA, the referee is the Office for Civil Rights — they make sure clinics follow the privacy rules.

### Question 4

HIPAA's rules apply to the people and places that handle health records as part of their job — like a doctor's office. They don't apply to just anyone.

### Question 5

There are three types of groups that must follow HIPAA: insurance plans, the companies that process claims, and doctor's offices that send health info electronically.

### Question 6

When a clinic hires an outside company to help with records, that helper company is a 'business associate.' They must promise to protect the information too.

### Question 7

PHI is the special name for health info that can be tied to one specific person — like a name plus a diagnosis together.

### Question 8

PHI is like a name tag plus a health detail. A list of 'common colds' with no names is fine, but 'Maria has the flu on June 1' is private.

### Question 9

Privacy doesn't care how the info is stored — on a computer, on paper, or spoken out loud. All of it is protected.

### Question 10

Some details are like fingerprints — they can point to exactly who a person is. A full-face photo is one of those, so it has to be removed to make info anonymous.

### Question 11

Some numbers are like a secret code that points to one single person. A medical record number is one of those, so it must be kept private.

### Question 12

To make health info truly anonymous, you have to remove every clue that could point to a person — 18 different kinds of clues in total.

### Question 13

There are two official ways to make health info anonymous: strip out all 18 clues, or have an expert prove that nobody could figure out who it is.

### Question 14

Your ZIP code can be a clue about who you are, especially in a small town. That's why it counts as identifying info that must be protected.

### Question 15

When you first visit a doctor, they hand you a paper that explains your privacy rights. That paper is the Notice of Privacy Practices.

### Question 16

Sometimes a patient doesn't want mail about their health sent home. They can ask the clinic to call their cell phone instead, and the clinic should honor that request.

### Question 17

Your health record is about you, so you are allowed to read it and get a copy — like being allowed to read your own report card.

### Question 18

If a patient spots a mistake in their chart, they can ask the office to fix it. The office reviews the request and either corrects it or explains in writing why not.

### Question 19

Privacy is your right to decide who sees your health details; confidentiality is the promise the clinic makes to keep those details safe.

### Question 20

The Security Rule is about the digital stuff — like patient info stored on computers — and the steps clinics must take to keep it safe from hackers.

### Question 21

Protecting computer records takes three kinds of care: rules people follow (administrative), locks and doors (physical), and passwords and software (technical).

### Question 22

Physical safeguards are the 'see and touch' protections — like turning a monitor so people walking by can't read private info.

### Question 23

Every clinic needs one person whose job is to be the 'privacy captain' — the person in charge of the rules that keep patient info safe.

### Question 24

Everyone who works at the clinic — from the doctor to the front-desk assistant — learns the privacy rules so everyone is on the same team protecting patients.

### Question 25

Imagine a library: you only get the books you need, not the whole library. Similarly, workers only see the patient info they need for their specific job.

### Question 26

If a worker only needs the answer to one question, you don't hand them the whole folder. You give just the page with the answer.

### Question 27

TPO is a shortcut for the three normal reasons a clinic shares info: to treat you, to get paid, and to run the office.

### Question 28

When the clinic sends your bill info to the insurance company so they'll pay, that's just 'payment' — it's allowed without extra permission.

### Question 29

If your doctor sends your file to the specialist you're seeing next, that's just part of taking care of you — no extra permission needed.

### Question 30

A clinic can use your info to care for you and get paid, but it can't sell your private health info to a stranger without your clear 'yes.'

### Question 31

A therapist's private notes are extra-private — like a locked diary. Even the rest of your chart doesn't automatically include them.

### Question 32

An 'accounting' is like a receipt showing who outside the clinic got to see your health info.

### Question 33

If a patient says 'please don't tell my sister my health details,' the office should respect that and write it down so everyone follows it.

### Question 34

If a clerk whispers but someone still overhears a little, that's an 'accident' the rules allow — as long as the clinic tried its best to keep things private.

### Question 35

A sign-in sheet is fine if it's just names — like signing in at school. It becomes a problem if it lists everyone's medical reason for visiting.

### Question 36

Saying 'Sarah, the doctor will see you now' is a normal part of a clinic. It's fine because only the name is shared, not health details.

### Question 37

Before you send a private paper by fax, double-check the number and put a note on top saying 'private' so the right person knows to keep it safe.

### Question 38

When a clinic hires an outside helper to handle records, they sign a special promise that the helper will protect the info too.

### Question 39

A 'breach' is when private health info gets out in a way it wasn't supposed to — like the wrong person seeing it.

### Question 40

If a clinic accidentally leaks private info, they have to tell the affected people quickly — within about two months at most.

### Question 41

If a big privacy leak affects lots of people in one state, the clinic has to tell the news and the government so everyone can protect themselves.

### Question 42

Smaller leaks get written in a yearly log and sent to the government once a year, instead of one by one.

### Question 43

Encryption is like a secret code on a computer that scrambles data so only the right person can read it.

### Question 44

When someone quits, you take back their key to the building — and their password to the computer system — right away.

### Question 45

If a patient's spouse is in the room and the patient doesn't mind, the clinic can talk with the spouse too. But if the patient says no, the clinic must stop.

### Question 46

Before emailing private health info, make sure you're sending it to the right person and using the office's safe, locked-down way of sending.

### Question 47

Before telling someone private info on the phone, make sure they really are who they say they are — like checking a secret code or asking questions only the real person would know.

### Question 48

Even after someone passes away, their health records stay private for 50 more years.

### Question 49

A 'personal representative' is the person who is legally allowed to make health decisions for someone else — like a parent for a child or a person with power of attorney.

### Question 50

If you pay cash and say 'please don't tell my insurance about this,' the clinic has to keep that visit a secret from your insurance.

### Question 51

Think of HIPAA as the minimum fence height. If your state wants a taller fence for privacy, the taller one wins.

### Question 52

HIPAA's rules apply to clinics, hospitals, and health plans — not to every company, like a life-insurance company.

### Question 53

Just because you have the key to the filing cabinet doesn't mean you can open your neighbor's folder. You can only look when your job needs you to.

### Question 54

If you see someone leaving private papers out in the open, you tell the person in charge so it gets fixed — you don't just look away.

### Question 55

The privacy notice is like a menu of your rights — you can ask for a copy anytime, and the office has to give it to you.

### Question 56

A hospital's front desk list can say 'Mr. Smith is in room 3 and doing okay,' but only if Mr. Smith was asked and didn't say no.

### Question 57

A clinic can't use your private health info to advertise products to you unless you clearly say yes in writing.

### Question 58

A clinic can ask you for donations using basic info like your name, but you can say 'stop asking me,' and they have to stop.

### Question 59

If a disease is dangerous and spreading, the clinic is allowed to tell the health department — that's for everyone's safety.

### Question 60

If someone may be getting hurt, the clinic is allowed — and usually must — tell the people who can help, even without permission.

### Question 61

The 'share only what's needed' rule has a big exception: doctors treating you can see what they need to give you good care.

### Question 62

A patient portal is like a private mailbox between the patient and the clinic — only the right person can open it.

### Question 63

Texting health info from a personal phone is like writing it on a postcard — it can be read by people it wasn't meant for.

### Question 64

Papers with private health info go through a shredder, not the normal garbage, so nobody can read them.

### Question 65

Leaving your computer open and unlocked is like leaving your diary open on a public counter — anyone can read it.

### Question 66

Your password is like your own signature — you never let someone else use it, because then nobody knows who really did what.

### Question 67

An audit trail is like a sign-in log that shows who opened a file and when — so snooping can be caught.

### Question 68

If an email asks for your secret password, it's like a stranger asking for your house key. Don't give it — tell a trusted adult (report it).

### Question 69

The Privacy Rule is the big privacy rule for everything; the Security Rule is the extra rule specifically about keeping computer records safe.

### Question 70

Breaking the privacy rules can cost a clinic a lot of money, and doing it on purpose can even mean serious legal trouble.

### Question 71

If someone thinks their privacy was broken, they complain to the special 'privacy referee' — the Office for Civil Rights.

### Question 72

It's against the rules to punish someone for speaking up about a privacy problem.

### Question 73

At the front desk, you talk about private stuff in a quiet voice, the way you'd whisper a secret instead of shouting it.

### Question 74

If a patient asks 'what does HIPAA do for me?', the assistant can say: 'It keeps your health info private and gives you rights to it' and show them the official notice.

### Question 75

The golden rule of privacy at work: only look at what you need, and always keep it safe — whether it's on a screen, on paper, or spoken out loud.
